releases.headline: Harden the startup HTTPS warning and directory-cleanup containment
releases.summary: Loopback classification for the not-HTTPS startup warning is now host-precise, and the empty-directory cleanup ascents are confined to strictly inside the upload tree.

items.title: Classify the startup HTTPS-warning's loopback exception by host, not substring
items.body: The boot-time 'rpOrigin is not HTTPS' warning is suppressed for a loopback origin. It previously tested for the substring 'localhost', so a value like http://localhost.evil.com counted as loopback and silenced the warning. The origin is now parsed and its host classified with the vendored SSRF guard, so only a genuine loopback host (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, and canonical spellings) suppresses the warning.

items.title: Confine the empty-directory cleanup ascents to inside the upload tree
items.body: The orphan-file and storage-migration cleanups walk up removing now-empty parent directories. Those ascents now stop strictly inside the upload / bundles directory — the orphan cleanup checks the full path separator so a sibling directory sharing the prefix can't match, and the storage migration re-checks containment with the vendored path-containment primitive on every step and fails closed on any escape.

items.title: Correct the documented TLS certificate auto-reload cadence
items.body: The docs described the Let's Encrypt certificate auto-reload as an hourly file poll; the server actually polls the certificate file every minute. The documentation now matches the implementation.

releases.headline: Add PKCE to Google sign-in
releases.summary: The Google authorization-code flow now uses PKCE, binding each authorization request to a session-side verifier.

items.title: Add PKCE to the Google authorization-code flow
items.body: Google sign-in now sends a PKCE code_challenge (S256 method) on the authorization request and presents the matching code_verifier — held only in the server-side session — at token exchange, per OAuth 2.1 and RFC 9700. An authorization code intercepted between Google and the callback can no longer be redeemed without the session's verifier, closing the authorization-code-injection vector that state alone does not cover. The token and userinfo requests also now surface a non-2xx response as the true HTTP status instead of parsing an error body as a success payload.

releases.headline: Encrypt chunked-upload fragments at rest
releases.summary: Chunked (large-file) uploads now stage every fragment as ciphertext, and the database overflow merge and settings overlay adopt prototype-pollution-safe property access.

items.title: Encrypt chunked-upload fragments at rest
items.body: A large-file upload is received in chunks that are staged on the scratch disk until the whole file arrives and is encrypted. Those fragments were previously written as plaintext for the duration of the upload — and up to a day for an abandoned upload before cleanup. Each chunk is now stored as XChaCha20-Poly1305 ciphertext under a per-upload key held only in memory, so no plaintext fragment ever lands on disk. An abandoned upload's on-disk fragments are unreadable ciphertext, and reassembly decrypts each chunk in order.

items.title: Prototype-pollution-safe property access on user-influenced keys
items.body: The database overflow-blob merge and the settings overlay build objects whose keys can be operator- or record-influenced. They now write and read those keys through the framework's prototype-pollution-safe own-property primitives, so a key named after a prototype member cannot re-parent the resulting object — defense-in-depth alongside the existing prototype-key stripping at parse time.

releases.headline: Fail-closed robustness for malformed certificates and truncated encrypted blobs
releases.summary: Three robustness fixes on the certificate, crypto-envelope, and backup-lock paths so a malformed input fails cleanly instead of crashing or leaking a raw library error.

items.title: Certificate fingerprinting no longer crashes on a malformed certificate
items.body: A certificate whose PEM body is non-empty but base64-decodes to zero bytes produced an empty re-encoding, and the line-wrapping step then threw a TypeError on the certificate-fingerprint / revocation path. It now yields a stable empty canonical form — which hashes deterministically and simply never matches a revocation entry — instead of throwing.

items.title: A truncated legacy encrypted blob fails with the typed envelope error
items.body: The legacy-format decrypt path had a dead length check that could never fire, so a blob whose ciphertext was shorter than the required 16-byte authentication tag fell through to a raw cipher-library error instead of the framework's typed 'Invalid envelope' error. The check now enforces the minimum tag length and fails closed with the typed error.

items.title: The backup/restore operation lock releases even if start-audit logging fails
items.body: The 'operation started' audit emit for a backup or restore now runs inside the lock's try/finally region, so the in-progress lock is released unconditionally — a start-audit failure can no longer leave the lock latched and wedge every subsequent backup and restore until a restart.

releases.headline: Bind Google sign-in to the stable account identity and harden the auth surface
releases.summary: Google sign-in now matches a returning account on its stable identity rather than the email alone, closing an account-takeover path, alongside several request-surface hardening fixes.

items.title: Bind returning Google sign-ins to the stable account identity
items.body: A returning Google sign-in is now matched to a stored account by its stable Google subject identifier, not the email address alone. A verified email can move between two distinct Google identities over time (a Workspace administrator reassigns a departed employee's address to a new hire, or a consumer account is deleted and the address later recreated), so a match on email with a different underlying identity is refused. A local password account can likewise no longer be signed into through Google merely because the addresses coincide. Both close an account-takeover path (email recycling and cross-provider assumption).

items.title: Rate-limit the passkey authentication-options endpoint
items.body: The unauthenticated passkey login-options endpoint — which runs a WebAuthn challenge operation and writes session state on every call — now carries the same per-minute rate limit as its verify sibling, so it can no longer be driven unbounded.

items.title: Fail loudly on a non-2xx response from Google
items.body: The Google token-exchange and userinfo requests now surface the true HTTP status on a non-2xx response instead of parsing the error or HTML body as if it were a success payload — which previously masked the real failure behind an opaque downstream error.

items.title: Constant-time key-fingerprint comparison and canonical loopback classification
items.body: The audit-archive verifier now compares signing-key fingerprints in constant time (matching the project-wide timing-safe comparison discipline), and the SSRF private-address check classifies loopback names through the vendored guard primitive rather than a bare literal, so every loopback spelling is treated consistently.

releases.headline: Keep uploaded content off disk and protect a restored backup
releases.summary: Uploaded file content is now parsed entirely in memory, and a backup restore can no longer be reverted by the exit-time database re-encrypt.

items.title: Refresh the vendored framework to 0.17.23
items.body: Update the vendored blamejs framework, picking up upstream session-security fixes — the session rotate and update-data paths now enforce the idle/absolute timeout floor (so a session past its idle timeout can no longer be revived by refreshing it), and a strict device-fingerprint policy with no request to compare against now fails closed — plus an audit-signature verifier that returns false on a malformed public key instead of throwing (hardening the backup-manifest verification the restore path relies on).

items.title: Parse uploads in memory so plaintext never lands on disk
items.body: File uploads are now parsed entirely in memory. Previously each uploaded part was streamed to a temporary file under the OS temp directory before HermitStash encrypted it, leaving unencrypted user content on the local filesystem for the duration of the request. The uploaded bytes now stay in RAM until they are sealed — closing that plaintext-at-rest window. Peak memory is unchanged; the upload pipeline already buffered the whole file.

items.title: Harden path containment with the framework's audited primitive
items.body: Custom-logo serving and local storage-path resolution now confine request-derived paths through the vendored path-containment primitive instead of a hand-rolled prefix check. The primitive correctly rejects a sibling-directory prefix escape (for example a path resolving just outside the upload directory whose name shares the directory's prefix) that a bare string prefix comparison could miss.

items.title: A backup restore is no longer reverted by the exit-time database re-encrypt
items.body: Restoring from a backup writes a fresh encrypted database and key file, then restarts the server. The graceful-shutdown step re-encrypts the in-memory working database back to disk — which could overwrite the just-restored file with the stale pre-restore copy (under the previous key), silently reverting the restore or leaving the next boot unable to open the database. The restore now suppresses that exit-time re-encrypt so the restored data is what boots.

items.title: Sealed-column queries and array updates stay correct
items.body: Paginated find and search now match a sealed column through its keyed blind index (and reject an unsupported operator on a sealed column loudly, instead of silently matching nothing). Appending an entry to a sealed array column now unseals the current array, appends, and reseals — preserving the existing entries and keeping the column encrypted rather than overwriting it in plaintext.

releases.headline: Refresh the vendored framework and keep key material out of error logs
releases.summary: A vendored-framework security refresh, together with hardening that stops secret key bytes from reaching error logs.

items.title: Refresh the vendored framework to 0.17.22
items.body: Update the vendored blamejs framework, picking up upstream security fixes: a quote-aware subjectAltName parser that closes a TLS hostname-verification bypass (a certificate could smuggle a hostname through a JSON-quoted SAN value), OIDC id_token verification that now requires a configured issuer to defend the cross-realm/cross-issuer case, RFC 8463 raw-key ed25519 DKIM interoperability, and a batch of cross-platform file-watch and daemon lifecycle fixes.

items.title: Suppress error text and stack traces on key-handling failure paths
items.body: Vault initialization, the boot-time envelope migration, the API-encrypt keypair load, and the vault / TLS / CA operator command-line tools no longer print an error message or stack trace that could embed raw private-key bytes when a key file is corrupt or a wrapped file fails to open (CWE-532). These paths now log only a non-secret error code, and any surfaced message is passed through a credential redactor first.

items.title: Clear two advisories in the test tooling
items.body: Update fast-uri and brace-expansion — development-only test dependencies, not shipped in the runtime image — to their patched releases, resolving a host-confusion and a denial-of-service advisory in the lint/test toolchain.

releases.headline: Refresh the runtime base image to drop the patched node-tar advisories
releases.summary: Repins the runtime base image to the current Chainguard rebuild, which carries npm's patched node-tar and current glibc.

items.title: Runtime base image repinned to the current patched rebuild
items.body: The digest-pinned Chainguard Node base image is advanced to the current rebuild, which ships npm's node-tar 12.0.0-r1 (resolving CVE-2026-59871, CVE-2026-59873, and CVE-2026-59874 — node-tar denial-of-service via a crafted PAX header, gzip bomb, or malformed archive) and glibc 2.43-r11. The base image is pinned by digest for reproducible builds; this bump is the base-OS patch path.

releases.headline: Audit-forwarding secret scrub and a stricter-DER vendored-framework refresh
releases.summary: A security-hardening patch. It adds a second-layer credential scrub to the audit events forwarded to a SIEM, and refreshes the vendored cryptography and identity framework to pick up a stricter DER length decoder on the shared certificate, CMS, and OCSP parse path.

items.title: Forwarded audit events scrub a recognized secret shape
items.body: When SIEM forwarding is enabled, a free-form audit detail now passes through a credential-shape scrub before it leaves the process, so a value matching a recognized secret shape (a PEM or SSH private key, a card number) is masked. The high-entropy content HS logs legitimately — content checksums, storage paths, and key prefixes — is left intact, so forensic context is preserved. Call sites already log prefixes and reasons rather than raw secrets; this is a second layer behind that discipline.

items.title: Refreshed the vendored cryptography and identity framework
items.body: The bundled framework is updated to its current release. The DER decoder that underlies every certificate, CMS, and OCSP parse now rejects a non-minimal length encoding, closing a BER/DER parser-differential an attacker could use to slip an alternate encoding of a certificate past a strict verifier.

releases.headline: Server-authoritative expiry, one-time enrollment-secret destruction, and a vendored-framework security refresh
releases.summary: A security-hardening release. Bundle retention becomes server-authoritative and individually-expired files stop being served or listed anywhere; one-time enrollment secrets are destroyed the moment they are delivered; chunked uploads gain an always-on scratch ceiling; and the vendored cryptography and identity framework is refreshed to its current release, bringing a broad batch of upstream fail-closed and injection hardening.

items.title: Bundle retention is server-authoritative
items.body: A bundle's expiry is now clamped to the operator's configured maximum. An uploader — including an anonymous one on the public drop page — can shorten a bundle's retention but can no longer request a window longer than the server allows, and every file in a bundle now expires together regardless of whether it arrived in a single request or in chunks. Previously a client could set an arbitrarily long retention, and a bundle's single-shot and chunked files could expire on different dates.

items.title: Individually-expired files are no longer served or listed
items.body: A file whose own expiry has passed is now withheld from the bundle browse page, the bundle JSON listing, the share page, and both the whole-bundle and per-folder ZIP downloads — matching the refusal the single-file download already returned. Previously such a file's bytes (through the ZIP paths) and its metadata (name, size, uploader) stayed reachable until the hourly sweep removed the record.

items.title: Enrollment provisioning secrets are destroyed at redemption
items.body: When a sync enrollment code is redeemed, its provisioning bundle — API key, client certificate and private key, and CA certificate — is now removed from the database the moment it is delivered to the client, rather than remaining on the redeemed row until the next hourly cleanup. The code stays single-use.

items.title: Chunked uploads bound their scratch space
items.body: Chunked upload now enforces an always-on per-bundle limit on staged (not-yet-assembled) chunk bytes, plus a per-file bound that applies even when an operator has lifted the file-size limit, so a stream of abandoned partial uploads can no longer exhaust the scratch disk. The abandoned-assembly cleanup now measures staleness from the last chunk actually written, so an active upload is never reclaimed mid-flight and a dormant one is reliably collected.

items.title: Empty values in encrypted columns carry tamper-evidence
items.body: An empty string stored in an encrypted database column is now sealed as an authenticated envelope rather than kept in the clear, so an attacker with database-write access cannot substitute a value for one.

items.title: Audit forwarding classifies events by exact action
items.body: When SIEM forwarding is enabled, each event's severity and outcome are derived from the exact action rather than a substring match. A refused or rate-limited event now surfaces as a warning a SIEM can alert on, and a deliberate administrative action such as lifting a suspension is no longer mislabeled as a failure.

items.title: Refreshed the vendored cryptography and identity framework
items.body: The bundled framework is updated to its current release, carrying a broad batch of upstream fail-closed and injection fixes across the cryptographic verifiers, the content and upload guards, the mail protocols, authentication, and request routing.

items.title: Sync file replacement preserves the prior file when it would exceed the size limit
items.body: Replacing a file in a sync bundle with a larger one that would push the bundle past its size limit now fails cleanly with the previous file intact. Previously the replacement deleted the old content and stored the new bytes before the limit was re-checked, so a rejected replacement reported failure while having already overwritten the file and left the bundle's size total understated.

items.title: Storage counters reflect reclaimed space after cleanup
items.body: Expired-file cleanup and empty-bundle removal now decrement the bundle and stash storage totals, so the admin dashboard's counts track space actually freed instead of drifting upward as files age out.

items.title: Bundle download count reflects real downloads
items.body: The whole-bundle ZIP download counter now increments only once at least one file has been packed, rather than on every request, so an aborted download or one where no file could be read no longer inflates the count.

items.title: Email template placeholders resolve declared values only
items.body: A template placeholder now resolves only an explicitly supplied value; a placeholder that names a built-in object property is left as literal text instead of rendering that property's contents.

releases.headline: Pulls the latest patched base-image packages at build time
releases.summary: The container image now upgrades every base-operating-system package to its latest patched build during the image build, instead of relying solely on the base image's own rebuild cadence. This closes the window where a freshly-published operating-system security fix has reached the package repository but not yet the rebuilt base image, so the image ships with the current patched packages. No configuration changes are required.

items.title: The image upgrades its base-OS packages to the latest patched build at build time
items.body: The build now runs an explicit package upgrade against the base image so it always ships the latest patched operating-system packages (for example a just-released glibc fix), independent of when the upstream base image is next rebuilt. Previously a security fix that had landed in the package repository but not yet in a rebuilt base image would ship unpatched until the base image caught up.

releases.headline: Refreshes the vendored framework, hardening redirect and header handling
releases.summary: A maintenance release that refreshes the vendored cryptography and identity framework to its current release. The refresh hardens the redirect and protocol-header handling HermitStash builds on — most visibly, a redirect target carrying a horizontal tab is now refused, closing an open-redirect a browser's URL parser would otherwise collapse to an attacker origin. No configuration changes are required.

items.title: Redirect targets reject a horizontal tab (open-redirect hardening)
items.body: The framework's redirect helper — which HermitStash's sign-in, OAuth, and admin flows use — now refuses a redirect target containing a horizontal tab, alongside the carriage-return, line-feed, and NUL it already rejected. A browser's URL parser strips a tab before resolving the address, so a target such as a tab followed by an authority would otherwise collapse to a protocol-relative address and navigate off-origin, slipping past the same-origin and allowlist checks. HermitStash inherits the fix by refreshing the framework.

items.title: Refreshed the vendored cryptography and identity framework
items.body: The vendored framework was updated to its current release, picking up its latest security and correctness hardening across the redirect, protocol-header, mail-authentication, federated-identity, and keychain primitives — including several fail-open and header-injection fixes in the paths HermitStash composes.

releases.headline: Security hardening across auth, uploads, backups, and the audit log
releases.summary: A broad security-hardening release. It closes fail-open and encoding-mismatch gaps in the sign-in, CSRF, session, single-use-code, upload, backup, and audit-log paths; refreshes the vendored cryptography and identity framework to its current release; and raises the minimum Node.js runtime to 24.18.0.

items.title: Google sign-in domain gate rejects malformed addresses
items.body: The allowed-domains gate for Google sign-in now validates the address and derives the domain from its final "@". A crafted address carrying more than one "@" (for example user@allowed.example@attacker.example) previously had its domain read from the wrong segment, so it could satisfy an allowed-domains restriction while its real mailbox was elsewhere. Such an address is now refused.

items.title: CSRF same-origin check canonicalizes both origins
items.body: The JSON/multipart cross-origin check now normalizes the browser Origin and the configured origin the same way (host case, default port, trailing dot, and internationalized labels) before comparing. A legitimate same-origin request can no longer be refused — nor a cross-site one accepted — because the two sides used different encodings of the same host.

items.title: Single-use email access codes are consumed atomically
items.body: Redeeming a one-time bundle access code now claims it with an atomic compare-and-set. Two simultaneous redemptions of the same code can no longer both succeed; the second is refused.

items.title: A stored file's content type is bound to its actual bytes
items.body: When an uploaded file's declared type is one the server renders inline (an image or PDF) but its magic bytes do not match, it is now stored as a generic download type instead of the spoofed inline type, so the serve-time preview cannot be steered by a false Content-Type regardless of the file extension. File downloads and previews also carry X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

items.title: Off-site backups exclude the plaintext upload scratch directory
items.body: The backup walk no longer copies the transient chunk-assembly scratch directory (pre-assembly upload chunks that are not yet application-encrypted) to the off-site backup bucket. Only encrypted stored content is backed up.

items.title: Encrypted audit-log export verifies the archive before returning rows
items.body: Exporting a decrypted audit-log archive now verifies the archive's post-quantum signature (pinned to this server's own key history) and recomputes its tamper chain before any row is returned. A rewritten or wrong-key archive is refused rather than exported as authentic.

items.title: Idempotency-Key replay cache is scoped to the authenticated principal
items.body: The Idempotency-Key replay cache slot is now bound to the requesting principal, so one client's key can no longer collide with another's — closing a cross-actor denial where a shared or guessed key blocked another principal from using it.

items.title: Session refresh enforces the configured timeout floors
items.body: Refreshing a session's activity now re-checks the configured idle and absolute timeout floors, so an expired session cannot be revived by continued activity, and an active one is not over-expired by the framework defaults.

items.title: Time-window gates fail closed on a malformed value
items.body: The brute-force lockout backoff, the pending two-factor deadline, and invite expiry now treat an absent or unparseable timestamp as expired/locked rather than letting a non-finite value silently disable the check. Disabling two-factor is now rate-limited like the other code-checking endpoints.

items.title: Admin IP blocklist canonicalizes IPv6 entries
items.body: An IPv6 address added to the admin block list is now canonicalized to the same form the runtime peer lookup produces, so a block written in an expanded or alternate compression form takes effect instead of silently never matching.

items.title: Reserved object keys are refused in settings and stored-record merges
items.body: Administrative settings dispatch and the database overflow-field merge now reject reserved prototype keys and resolve entries by own-property lookup, so a request-supplied key cannot re-parent an object or pass an inherited member off as a known setting.

items.title: Untrusted paths and email headers route through the hardened primitives
items.body: Restore-time upload paths are resolved through the shared safe-path primitive, and email address validation and subject composition through the shared header-safety primitive that rejects carriage-return, line-feed, and NUL — closing header-injection and traversal classes at their source. API-key scope selection now matches whole scopes rather than a substring.

items.title: Minimum Node.js runtime raised to 24.18.0
items.body: The runtime floor is now Node.js 24.18.0 (24.17.0 was a security release; 24.18.0 bundles SQLite 3.53.1 and a backup-path fix, and guarantees the OpenSSL 3.5 post-quantum signature surface).

items.title: Refreshed the vendored cryptography and identity framework
items.body: The vendored cryptography and identity framework was updated to its current release, picking up its security hardening for HTTP message signatures, mail authentication, path-scoped routing, single-use token concurrency, and recursion and header-injection defenses.

items.title: Folder ZIP downloads use a query parameter for the folder path
items.body: The in-bundle folder download link now carries the folder path as a query parameter. The router refuses an encoded path separator in the request path, so nested folders are addressed via the query string rather than an encoded path segment.

items.title: Run Node.js 24.18.0 or newer
items.body: Upgrade the runtime to Node.js 24.18.0+ before deploying this release. The Docker image already pins a matching runtime; only non-container deployments need to act.

releases.headline: Real-time SIEM forwarding for the audit log
releases.summary: Stream every audit event to a SIEM as it happens over syslog or an HTTP webhook, with secret- and PII-shaped values stripped before anything leaves the host.

items.title: SIEM forwarding for audit events
items.body: Forward every audit event to a SIEM in real time over RFC 5424 syslog (udp / tcp / tls) or an HTTP webhook (Splunk HEC, Datadog, Grafana Loki, or any JSON-ingest endpoint, with bearer / basic / header auth). Each event carries the structured who / what / when / where / how — actor, target, source IP, method and path, auth class, user-agent, and request id. Security failures forward at warn severity so a SIEM can alert on them; secret- and PII-shaped values (tokens, keys, card numbers) are stripped before the event leaves the host. Webhook delivery batches and retries on transient errors, tuned for near-real-time forwarding. Configure it under Audit Log settings or via the SIEM_* environment variables, and use the built-in connectivity test to send a probe event and confirm the endpoint before relying on it. Off by default.

items.title: Enabling SIEM forwarding captures full IP and user-agent
items.body: A SIEM is only useful with the real source IP, so turning on forwarding automatically enables full-IP and user-agent capture and locks both on while it is active. The stored audit log and the forwarded stream stay consistent — an investigator never receives a hashed IP in their SIEM. Disable forwarding to return both capture toggles to your control.

items.title: Registration audit events recorded the email as an unreadable blob
items.body: A new account's registration event stored the account email as an encrypted value instead of the address itself, so searching the audit log by that email missed the registration row and the forwarded event was not actionable. Registration and sign-in events now record the plaintext email consistently.

releases.headline: Encrypted, signed on-disk audit archival
releases.summary: Optional size-based rotation moves the oldest audit entries to encrypted, post-quantum-signed bundles on disk, keeping the database lean while preserving a verifiable trail.

items.title: Size-based encrypted audit archival
items.body: When the audit log exceeds a configurable row threshold, the oldest entries are moved to a passphrase-encrypted (Argon2id + XChaCha20-Poly1305), post-quantum-signed bundle on disk and pruned from the database, with the tamper-evidence chain re-anchored so the live log still verifies. Every bundle is read back and verified end-to-end before any rows are pruned, so a failed write never loses data. Manage archives from the audit viewer: list them, verify a bundle (signature + checksum + full chain recompute), trigger a run on demand, and decrypt a bundle for export as CSV, JSON, or CADF. Enable it, set the threshold, and set the bundle passphrase under Audit Log settings, which also exposes the tamper-evidence chain toggle.

releases.headline: Decrypt and export the audit log
releases.summary: Admins can download the decrypted audit trail in CSV, JSON, or CADF format for investigation, SIEM ingestion, or compliance.

items.title: Audit log export
items.body: Export the decrypted audit trail from the audit viewer, honoring the current search and date filters. Choose CSV (formula-injection-safe, for spreadsheets), JSON (the full structured entries), or CADF — a Cloud Auditing Data Federation event batch that SIEM and compliance tooling can ingest. Each export is admin-gated and is itself recorded in the audit log.

releases.headline: Full request context in the audit log and an Audit Log settings panel
releases.summary: Audit entries now record the full who / what / when / where / how of each action, with an admin panel to control IP visibility, user-agent capture, and retention.

items.title: Full request context on every audit entry
items.body: Audit entries now record the request method and path, the authentication type (session, API key, or anonymous), the client user-agent (when enabled), and a request id, alongside the existing performer, target, and source IP. The audit viewer groups each entry into a who / what / when / where / how breakdown on click, and the search box now also matches on IP, path, and user-agent. The added fields that carry identifiers (path, user-agent) are encrypted at rest and shown decrypted to admins.

items.title: Audit Log settings panel
items.body: A new admin Settings tab controls the audit log: set a retention period in days or keep entries indefinitely; record full IP addresses for investigations (off by default — otherwise the source IP is stored as a one-way hash the operator cannot reverse); and capture the client user-agent. The IP and user-agent settings apply to new entries only — values already stored as a hash stay private.

releases.headline: Admin dialogs no longer clip controls under the scrollbar
releases.summary: Scrollable admin dialogs now reserve space for the scrollbar so right-edge controls stay fully visible.

items.title: Right edge of admin dialogs clipped by the scrollbar
items.body: The customer-stash editor and the per-user limits dialog reserved no space for their scrollbar, so on browsers that draw an overlay scrollbar (Windows 11, macOS) the right edge of controls — unit selectors, No-limit checkboxes — could sit under it. Both dialogs now reserve a scrollbar gutter, and the per-user limits dialog stays within the viewport on short screens instead of overflowing.

releases.headline: No-limit option for per-user and per-stash upload caps
releases.summary: Upload-limit overrides can now lift a cap entirely instead of only retuning it, on both individual users and customer stash pages.

items.title: Mark a per-user upload cap as No limit
items.body: Each per-user override — storage quota, max file size, max bundle size, max file count, and allowed extensions — now has a No-limit toggle in the user-limits dialog. A blank field still falls back to the global default; No limit removes the cap for that user, letting an admin grant an individual user a higher ceiling than the instance-wide setting. A No-limit storage quota also overrides a configured global per-user quota, and marking allowed extensions No limit accepts any file type for that user.

items.title: No-limit upload caps on customer stash pages
items.body: The stash editor gains the same No-limit toggle on max file size, max bundle size, max files, and allowed extensions. It now also exposes a Max Bundle Size field, which previously had no control.

items.title: Reorganized the stash editor
items.body: The customer-stash editor is wider and grouped into Page, Access, Upload limits, and Sync sections for a clearer layout.

items.title: Updated vendored framework
items.body: Refreshed the vendored blamejs dependency to its latest release.

releases.headline: Per-user upload limits and storage quotas, set from the admin user list
releases.summary: Administrators can now tailor upload limits and a storage quota to an individual user, overriding the instance-wide defaults only where needed.

items.title: Per-user upload limits and storage quotas
items.body: Set a storage quota, maximum file size, maximum bundle size, maximum file count, and an allowed-extension list on any user from the admin user list. Every field is blank by default and falls back to the global configuration when left unset, so the limits stay off until you set them. Overrides apply to that user's own uploads; uploads made through a customer stash keep the stash's own limits. Each change is recorded in the audit log.

releases.headline: Share a customer stash with individual users, no team required
releases.summary: A customer stash can now grant read access to its uploads to individual user accounts directly, without first creating a team. An administrator adds users to a stash by email, and each assigned user sees that customer's uploads on their dashboard under a new "Shared with me" section. The existing team assignment still works, and a stash can be shared with a team and individual users at the same time.

items.title: Assign individual users to a customer stash
items.body: The stash editor now has a "Users with access" control: an administrator adds user accounts by email and removes them at any time. Assigned users get read access to that stash's uploads. This is independent of teams — a stash no longer needs a team just to share its files with a specific person, and it can be shared with a team and individual users simultaneously. Member changes are audited, and a user's access is fully revoked the moment they are removed.

items.title: Dashboard "Shared with me" section
items.body: A user who has been added to one or more customer stashes sees a "Shared with me" section on their dashboard listing those stashes and the uploads in each, with open and ZIP-download actions. The list only ever shows stashes the user was explicitly added to.

releases.headline: Storage quotas hold under concurrent uploads
releases.summary: The global, per-account, and per-vault storage caps are now enforced on the committed total rather than a snapshot taken before the upload is written, so a burst of simultaneous uploads can no longer slip past a cap by each reading the same pre-write usage. The per-bundle file-count and size caps already worked this way; the global and per-account caps now get the same authoritative post-write check, and an upload that pushes a cap over is rolled back and rejected.

items.title: Global and per-account storage caps are enforced against concurrent overruns
items.body: Storage-quota checks read the current usage, then wrote the file a moment later — so several uploads arriving at once each saw the same pre-write total, all passed, and together exceeded the configured cap by the size of the in-flight batch. The global storage quota and the per-account quota are now re-checked on the committed total after each file lands (the same way the per-bundle file-count and size limits already were); a file that pushes a cap over is removed and the upload rejected. The single-file, chunked, and vault upload paths all enforce this, so an operator's disk and fair-use ceilings hold under concurrency. Caps left unset stay disabled and add no overhead.

references.label: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource (Race Condition)
